articles.title: Psychology says children who tell one parent everything but hide things from the other may not always be about who they feel closer to
articles.summary: “Mom already knows.” “Dad doesn't need to know.” Some children seem to have a clear choice about which parent gets to hear the full story.
articles.body: “Mom already knows.” “Dad doesn't need to know.” Some children seem to have a clear choice about which parent gets to hear the full story. They may talk freely with one parent about school, friends, mistakes, crushes, arguments or something embarrassing that happened during the day. But when the other parent asks the same question, the conversation suddenly becomes much shorter. It can leave parents wondering: Why does my child tell them everything but barely tell me anything? Research on parent-child disclosure suggests that children do not necessarily share the same information with both parents. The difference can depend on the subject, the relationship they have with each parent and, importantly, how they expect the parent to respond.Children learn what happens after they talkA child does not need to consciously think, “Mum will react better than Dad” every time they decide whom to approach. They may have learned it through repeated experiences. If one parent usually listens first, asks questions and helps the child work through a problem, the child may come to expect that kind of response. If the other parent tends to become angry, lecture them, immediately look for a solution or turn a small mistake into a larger discussion, the child may become more selective about what they share. Research has found a link between parental reactions and later disclosure.A study involving 982 young people examined how parents' positive and negative reactions to disclosure were related to children's information-sharing. Negative reactions were associated with feeling more controlled and less connected to parents, which was then linked with increased secrecy and less disclosure. Positive reactions were associated with greater connection and more disclosure. That does not mean one angry conversation makes a child stop talking forever. It suggests that patterns of response can shape what children decide to share over time.A child may not tell both parents the same thingsThe subject itself can also matter. A 2006 study of 276 adolescents and their parents found that adolescents disclosed more to mothers than fathers, particularly about personal matters. Greater trust and parental acceptance were associated with more disclosure and less secrecy. A newer study of 214 middle adolescents also found different patterns of disclosure to mothers and fathers. The largest group in the study disclosed more to mothers than fathers, particularly about personal and multifaceted issues. So a child telling one parent about a friendship problem while saying nothing to the other does not automatically mean they love or trust one parent more. They may simply feel that one parent is easier to approach about that particular subject.“What will happen if I tell them?”For children, the expected reaction can be as important as the information itself. Imagine a child who has received a poor test score. With one parent, they may expect: “Let's see what went wrong.” With the other, they may expect: “How could you get this mark?” Even before the conversation happens, that expectation can affect whether the child starts talking. Research on 118 early and middle adolescents found that concerns about parental disapproval were one reason adolescents chose not to disclose certain behaviours. For personal matters, some adolescents considered the information private or not harmful enough to share. The study also found that better parent-child relationships were associated with fuller disclosure. This becomes particularly relevant as children grow older. They start making more decisions about what they consider personal and how much parents need to know.One parent can become the child's first choiceThere can also be much simpler reasons for the difference. One parent may be around more during bedtime. Another may drive the child to school every morning. One may regularly help with homework, while the other spends more time playing or talking at dinner. Small, repeated interactions can make one parent the person the child naturally approaches. Research supports the importance of responsiveness in these conversations. A seven-day study involving 109 mother-adolescent pairs found that adolescents disclosed more to their mothers on days when they perceived their mothers as more responsive than usual.What parents should not doFinding out that a child tells the other parent more can hurt. But turning it into an accusation may make the child even less willing to talk. Questions such as “Why do you tell your mother everything but me?” or “Don't you trust me?” can shift the conversation away from what the child was trying to share and towards the parent's feelings. A calmer response can leave the door open: “You can tell me things even if you're worried about how I'll react.” “If you think I'll be upset, you can tell me that too.” “I'm listening. Tell me what happened.” And when the child finally shares something, the first response does not always have to be advice. Sometimes listening without immediately correcting, judging or solving the problem gives the child a reason to come back next time.A child does not have to tell both parents exactly the same things. They may talk to one parent about friendships and another about school. They may tell one parent about an embarrassing incident but go to the other when they are angry. As children become teenagers, they may also consider some parts of their lives personal. That is not automatically a problem. The bigger concern is when a child consistently hides important information because they are afraid of a parent's reaction, expect punishment or believe they will not be heard.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A New Hampshire groundskeeper lived a remarkably simple life in a mostly empty mobile home, spending his days mowing lawns and doing odd jobs for
articles.body: A New Hampshire groundskeeper lived a remarkably simple life in a mostly empty mobile home, spending his days mowing lawns and doing odd jobs for residents at a trailer park in the small town of Hinsdale. Geoffrey Holt rarely drew attention to himself and was often seen riding his lawn mower around town or sitting quietly by a nearby brook. But after his death in June 2023 at the age of 82, residents discovered that the unassuming caretaker had quietly built a multimillion-dollar fortune through investments. Holt’s will left $3.8 million to Hinsdale, a community of about 4,200 people, with instructions that the money should benefit local education, health, recreation and culture.New Hampshire groundskeeper led a simple life with little interest in wealthHolt lived at Stearns Park, a mobile-home community where he worked as a caretaker. Residents knew him for wearing threadbare clothes, mowing lawns and travelling around on his mower. His trailer contained very little furniture, and he did not own a television or computer. According to his friend Edwin “Smokey” Smith, Holt seemed to have everything he wanted because he simply did not want very much.Holt had previously worked at a grain mill in nearby Brattleboro, Vermont, and had also taught driver's education and social studies earlier in his life. He later stopped driving and relied on a bicycle and, eventually, his lawn mower to get around. Mowing was more than a job for him. A therapist who knew Holt said he appeared to see it as a way of being outdoors and providing a service to people he cared about.The fortune nobody knew aboutAlthough Holt lived frugally, he had been investing his money for decades. His friend Smith, who later became executor of his estate, knew that Holt's investments were doing well, but even he was surprised by the size of the fortune Holt had accumulated.Holt's investments included mutual funds, and he regularly read financial publications. He also spent his money on personal interests rather than an extravagant lifestyle, collecting hundreds of model cars and train sets, books and records. His collection included works related to history, as well as music by composers including Handel and Mozart.$3.8m left to the townHolt died in June 2023, and his will contained a simple but extraordinary instruction: $3.8 million was to go to the town of Hinsdale to benefit the community in education, health, recreation and culture. The gift came as a surprise to many residents who had known him for years but had no idea he had accumulated such wealth.Steve Diorio, who chaired Hinsdale's selectboard, described the gift as tremendous, particularly because Holt had chosen to leave his fortune to the town where he had spent much of his life. The money was expected to provide a lasting source of support for the community rather than being spent all at once.How Hinsdale planned to use the moneyRather than immediately spending the entire inheritance, Hinsdale planned to establish a trust through the New Hampshire Charitable Foundation and use the investment income to support community projects. At the time the gift was reported, officials estimated that the fund could generate about $150,000 a year.Residents suggested several possible uses, including repairing the clock on Town Hall, restoring local buildings and purchasing a new ballot-counting machine. Another idea was to create an online driver's education course, an especially fitting possibility given Holt's earlier work teaching students to drive.A legacy that reflected how he livedHolt's sister, Alison, said her brother had always been frugal and did not need much to be happy. She recalled that their father had emphasised saving and investing, values that Holt appears to have carried throughout his life.Holt also had a strong connection to Hinsdale. He rarely travelled far and developed friendships within the mobile-home community. After suffering a stroke a few years before his death, he had mobility problems and could no longer mow lawns as he once did. His decision to leave his fortune to the town therefore became a final way of supporting the community where he had quietly lived for decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit appointed new IAF chief, to take over from Oct 31
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The govt has appointed Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, currently serving as Vice Chief of the Air Staff, as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff, in the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The govt has appointed Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, currently serving as Vice Chief of the Air Staff, as the 29th Chief of the Air Staff, in the rank of Air Chief Marshal, with effect from Oct 31, 2026. He will succeed Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh, who superannuates on Oct 31.An experimental test pilot and qualified flying instructor with over 3,500 hours of flying experience, Air Marshal Dixit has held key operational and strategic appointments, including CISC, HQ IDS and AOC-in-C, Central Air CommandThe Air Marshal has extensive flying experience on various aircraft, including Mirage-2000, variants of MiG, HPT-32, An-32, Avro, Kiran, Jaguar, IL-78, Hawk, and Tejas.During his service career, spanning approximately four decades, he has been actively involved in numerous operations and exercises, viz. Op Safed Sagar, Op Rakshak, Cope-India and Op Sindoor. Widely known for pushing the indigenous LCA Tejas and other indigenous aircraft projects in the force, Air Marshal Dixit is expected to further promote the Aatmanirbharta initiative of the govt.

articles.title: ‘Vote loot’: Bengal Congress Demands total re-polling in Nandigram, Rejinagar over irregularities
articles.summary: KOLKATA: The Bengal Congress on Tuesday demanded fresh polling in the Nandigram and Rejinagar assembly constituencies, alleging intimidation of voters,
articles.body: KOLKATA: The Bengal Congress on Tuesday demanded fresh polling in the Nandigram and Rejinagar assembly constituencies, alleging intimidation of voters, removal of its polling agents and widespread electoral malpractice during the bypolls.State Congress president Subhankar Sarkar alleged that party agents had been forcibly removed from polling booths in Rejinagar and claimed that several booths in Nandigram had been “captured” by workers of the ruling BJP.The Congress’s Rejinagar candidate Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi staged a sit-in outside the local police station, seeking cancellation of the polling and fresh elections, Sarkar said at a press conference at the party’s state headquarters, Bidhan Bhavan, in Kolkata.“Our Rejinagar candidate has begun a sit-in before the local PS protesting the forcible eviction of our agents from over a hundred booths in that constituency. Later we found that Congress agents were roughed up and forced to leave from almost all the booths in Rejinagar,” Sarkar alleged.He claimed that the party had alerted the Election Commission on Monday night about an alleged conspiracy to rig the election, purportedly involving the inspector-in-charge of the Rejinagar police station and officials at different levels of the administration."An atmosphere of intimidation has been created in such a manner that except the BJP workers, no one else can stay inside the polling booths,” Sarkar added.In Nandigram, Congress candidate Milan Pradhan alleged that the polling process was marred by intimidation of voters and alleged bias by the police and security forces.Pradhan, who is currently out on interim bail granted by the Calcutta high court in connection with cases arising from the 2007 anti-land acquisition agitation in Nandigram, also alleged that police attempted to restrict his movement during polling.“A climate of hooliganism and utter lawlessness is prevailing in Nandigram for the past few days. Miscreants are moving around on motorcycles at night and threatening my agents and supporters not to come out and vote. They have snatched the identity cards of my poll agents,” he told PTI Videos.Pradhan also alleged that women voters had been prevented from entering polling stations and claimed that their voter slips were taken away.“Nearly a hundred women from the Rajaram Chowk area had come to me alleging that their voter slips were snatched outside polling stations by a group of people who forcibly turned them back, saying their votes have already been cast. These are clear signs of looting of votes and trampling of democracy. Places where people have been able to cast their votes have spoken against the government,” he added.He further alleged that police and CRPF personnel had prevented him from moving freely in the constituency.“The police have taken up the task of making people vote in favour of the ruling BJP,” he said, alleging that shops of minority voters were being looted while police remained silent.Pradhan claimed that he had submitted several complaints to the Election Commission but expressed doubts about getting relief from the poll panel.“The Commission is also working for the government. Gyanesh Kumar is actually Vanish Kumar, who is controlled by the BJP headquarters. We have lodged our complaints before the EC because that is an official procedure, but we are not hopeful of receiving justice from the poll body,” he said.The Congress has demanded total re-polling in both Nandigram and Rejinagar.Sarkar also claimed that the BJP was controlling the polling mechanism in Nandigram and alleged that no Election Commission official or observer was present there.The reference to Gyanesh Kumar as “Vanish Kumar” has been used previously by the Trinamool Congress during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. The TMC used the term while accusing the Chief Election Commissioner of making people’s voting rights “vanish”.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: UK arrests seventh man over alleged RAF Fairford air base terror plot
articles.summary: British police have arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offence over a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US military base in
articles.body: British police have arrested a 22-year-old man in London on suspicion of a terror offence over a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US military base in western England that has been used by American bombers in strikes against Iran.Counter Terrorism Policing said on Tuesday that the British national was detained in Westminster, central London, and that officers had searched a property in the area. He remains in custody.The arrest is the seventh in the investigation into the suspected plot. Six men arrested previously, including a British-Iranian dual national detained on October 1, have been released on bail under investigation."This remains a live investigation and our specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF Fairford," senior national coordinator for counter terrorism policing Vicki Evans said, according to news agency Reuters.Evans added that detectives “continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry” and “remain committed to investigating all possible angles.”The investigation began after five men were detained shortly after midnight on September 27 following reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford. Armed police and army bomb-disposal experts were deployed, while scores of residents living near the base were evacuated.Police later said they found a quantity of an accelerant - gasoline - in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives.A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later in central London on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. All six previously arrested suspects have since been released on bail.Laurence Taylor, head of UK counter terrorism policing, said the suspects face stringent bail conditions and “absolutely remain under investigation”.British authorities have said there are indications that Iran may have been involved. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK sees “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, but did not provide details about what the suspects were allegedly planning or why Tehran was believed to be involved.Taylor said investigators were examining whether the suspected offences were committed by “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”Iran has denied involvement. Its embassy in the UK condemned what it described as “unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets” linking Tehran to the suspected plot.The incident has also drawn attention in Washington. US president Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford. He said those behind the threat “would be linked to Iran”, but offered no details.“We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” Trump said.US vice president JD Vance said the bombers were removed “out of an abundance of caution”.“We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well. So, we are being extremely cautious," he said.US secretary of state Marco Rubio, however, downplayed a direct connection between the bomber redeployment and the British investigation, saying: “It’s not unusual to see rotations happen and moving into the different parts of the world based on exercises.”You use AI every day. articles.summary: US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy alleged that an \"unprecedented and unconstitutional\" effort is underway to conceal the impact of the Iran war after the
articles.body: US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy alleged that an "unprecedented and unconstitutional" effort is underway to conceal the impact of the Iran war after the Department of Defense allegedly denied him access to Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, a key US military base in the Middle East.Al Udeid Air Base has repeatedly come under attack from Iran during the war launched by the US and Israel in February."This trip confirmed for me that there is an active, unprecedented, unconstitutional effort underway to hide the costs of this war and the implications of this war from Congress and the American people," Murphy told a small group of journalists in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, the second stop on his trip.He also claimed that the Pentagon refused to arrange a briefing for him on the war while he was in the region."I've never encountered anything like this in my time in the Senate, and it's part of a deliberate campaign of obfuscation that my Republican colleagues in Congress should demand an end to," he said.Murphy made clear, however, that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had facilitated his visit, including arranging meetings with diplomats, a stance he contrasted with that of the Pentagon, led by Pete Hegseth.During his trip, Murphy met with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, as well as other senior Gulf officials.(With Reuters inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: AI models are misbehaving, but America still won’t slow down. China is a big reason why
articles.summary: Imagine building one of the most powerful technologies on Earth and then asking everyone to slow down.
articles.body: Imagine building one of the most powerful technologies on Earth and then asking everyone to slow down.That is the strange position Dario Amodei has put himself in as the AI industry barrels towards its next frontier. On October 4, Donald Trump created a new “Super Intelligence Force” to help ensure continued American dominance, barely three weeks after the Anthropic chief executive called for frontier AI development to be paced more carefully. What looks like a policy dispute is becoming something larger: A fight over who gets to decide how fast the technology moves.Amodei set out his case on September 12 in a 3,800-word essay titled ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, arguing that AI development is moving faster than the safeguards needed to control it. He called for independent evaluators to have deep access to frontier labs and for democratic countries to coordinate on safety standards. OpenAI's Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis all backed the direction of his argument.Donald Trump reacted very differently. On September 14, he called fears about AI taking over the world a ‘HOAX’ and described opposition to AI and data centres as a ‘SICK conspiracy’, arguing that China was the only country that would benefit from tighter controls. His message was simple: America cannot afford to slow while China is still racing to catch up.The clash is bigger than a disagreement between a president and a tech chief. The people building frontier AI are increasingly talking about brakes, while the US government is building the infrastructure, capital base and geopolitical machinery to keep the accelerator down, and the technology itself is beginning to give both sides reasons to worry.The people building AI are asking for brakesAmodei's proposal is not a call for America to surrender its lead. He wants the US and its allies to stay ahead of China, maintain restrictions on the most advanced chips reaching Beijing and act against the unauthorised distillation of frontier models.What he wants to change is the speed and manner of development.His concern is that frontier labs are being pushed into a race where releasing a more capable model first can be worth billions, while delaying it for safety work can mean losing the market. That creates an obvious problem when the systems are becoming more autonomous and capable of operating with less human supervision.Amodei pointed to the July cyberattack involving OpenAI agents and warned that, within six to 12 months, a swarm of similar systems could potentially take over much of the internet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage without adequate safeguards.Altman said OpenAI would commit to independent evaluation. Musk simply said, ‘Dario is right’. Hassabis said the essay pointed in the right direction. That was striking because the leaders of the biggest AI companies rarely agree on much beyond the need to build faster and bigger.There is a sceptical camp too. Yann LeCun, one of the pioneers of modern AI, told Fortune that Amodei was ‘deluded’ and ‘crazy’ and argued that many of the recent incidents were failures of human oversight and cybersecurity rather than evidence that AI was spiralling out of control.The disagreement is important because both sides are looking at the same evidence and drawing different conclusions. One sees a technology becoming difficult to contain. The other sees badly designed systems that can still be fixed.AI as real estate?Trump's response becomes easier to understand when AI is viewed not as a chatbot but as a vast construction project.The US already dominates hyperscale data-centre infrastructure. Fifteen of the world's 20 largest hyperscale data-centre markets are in the US, according to Synergy Research Group, now part of TechInsights. Northern Virginia and the greater Beijing area alone account for 17% of global hyperscale capacity.Trump wants that lead to become permanent.In January 2025, he stood beside Altman, Oracle's Larry Ellison and SoftBank's Masayoshi Son to announce Stargate, a plan that could eventually put $500bn into US AI infrastructure. Trump, drawing directly on his property background, described the data centres as ‘big, beautiful buildings’ and reminded reporters that he had been in the real estate business.The description was more revealing than it sounded. AI may appear weightless on a screen, but the race depends on extremely physical things: land, electricity, cooling systems, chips, transmission lines and permission to build.That is why data centres have become a political issue. A Heatmap survey in August found that 75% of Americans would oppose a new data centre being built near where they live, including 61% who strongly oppose it. Trump has floated the idea of giving communities that host them a financial dividend.The politics are particularly important with the November midterms approaching. AI is no longer only about future superintelligence. It is about power bills, land use, jobs and whether a giant industrial facility appears behind someone's house.Then OpenAI started hitting the brakesThe strongest evidence for Amodei's case is not a prediction about what AI might do one day. It is what frontier systems are doing now.On September 27, OpenAI paused training of its latest models after agents behaved unexpectedly while searching US government websites. It was the second development pause in three months. The first followed the July incident involving OpenAI agents and Hugging Face. The company said it would resume training only after adding more safeguards.The incidents went beyond a laboratory. On September 24, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to the public-facing Medicare statistics portal and accessed both public and non-public files. He said no personal information was believed to have been accessed, while a forensic investigation continued.Then, on September 28, OpenAI scrapped the planned launch of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal testing found that the model could take actions beyond its instructions and fail to accurately communicate what it had done. The Washington Post reported that the company had also paused work on highly capable models because it lacked sufficient safeguards.None of this proves that AI is about to escape human control. But it does prove something less cinematic and more important: The companies themselves increasingly believe there are points at which development has to stop until the safety systems catch up.The economics make stopping harderThe strange part is that the AI business is not showing signs of running out of demand.OpenAI's annualised revenue was approaching $70bn by late September, according to Axios, after growing more than 70% since the beginning of the third quarter. Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached about $65bn in July, according to figures cited by Axios and the New York Times.Epoch AI researchers Josh You and Lynette Bye argue that OpenAI and Anthropic are growing as fast as, or faster than, almost any companies of their size in history. That matters because a company growing that quickly has a powerful reason to keep spending and keep releasing.Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows the other side of the equation. Reuters reported $4.59bn in 2025 revenue, a roughly $42bn net loss and about $20bn in cash, alongside $518bn in future cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations. About $34bn of the loss came from accounting charges, while the operating loss was more than $8bn. The $518bn is not conventional debt. It is a vast commitment to future computing power.So this is not quite a bust. It is a gigantic bet that needs to keep paying off.That resembles the dotcom era. The crash destroyed fortunes, but much of the fibre-optic infrastructure built during the boom remained and became part of the internet economy that followed. AI could experience the same pattern: Some companies fail, some infrastructure proves excessive, but the underlying technology keeps advancing.China is the wall behind the acceleratorFor Washington, there is one fact that makes Amodei's idea extremely difficult to implement: China.The US still holds major advantages in advanced semiconductors, computing infrastructure and access to frontier chips. But the gap in model capability has narrowed sharply. Recent assessments put leading Chinese systems only months behind American ones in several areas.That means the US cannot easily decide to pause on its own and expect the rest of the world to follow.Amodei accepts this problem. His argument is effectively that democratic countries should pace themselves while maintaining enough of a technological lead over authoritarian rivals. But that creates a narrow window. Slow down too little and safety efforts achieve little. Slow down too much and China could close the gap.The nuclear age produced a similar dilemma. After the Second World War, Washington proposed the Baruch Plan for international control of atomic energy. The proposal failed, distrust deepened and the arms race followed. Only after the Cuban missile crisis did Washington and Moscow begin building more practical communication and arms-control mechanisms.AI is not a nuclear weapon, but the incentive problem is familiar. A country can believe a technology is dangerous and still believe falling behind would be more dangerous.That is why the US-China AI dialogue matters. During Xi Jinping's September visit to Washington, the two sides agreed to establish a channel for AI-related incidents and continue discussions on AI safety. It is a small step, but also an echo of an older lesson: When two powers are racing with technologies capable of causing accidents, communication becomes a form of insurance.The White House accord is the testTrump's answer to the safety debate so far is not a slowdown. It is self-regulation.On September 29, the White House unveiled its Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by Trump and leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia. The companies committed to four layers of controls: internal monitoring, an internal safety team, an independent external auditor and an independent board committee overseeing the process.The important detail is what the accord does not contain.There is no regulator overseeing the auditors. Each company is responsible for its own controls, auditor and board oversight. There are no penalties for breaking the pledge and no deadline for completing the measures. The document says that, over time, governments may turn the principles into law.Trump called the agreement ‘morally binding’. That may be enough while everyone agrees. The harder test comes when a safety measure costs a company billions, delays a model or allows a rival to release first.The idea of voluntary restraint has appeared before. Scientists at the 1975 Asilomar conference agreed to safety guidelines for recombinant DNA research and then continued the work. The difference now is the scale of the commercial prize and the presence of a strategic rival.So where does the race go next?On October 4, Trump created a ‘Super Intelligence Force’ headed by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. The group will study the risks and opportunities of advanced AI and report to Trump within 120 days, while its stated mission is to ensure continued American leadership.That is not a government preparing to step away from the race. It is a government trying to build a bigger car while installing a better dashboard.The next phase will therefore be defined by a strange competition inside the competition. AI companies need to grow quickly enough to satisfy investors and stay ahead of rivals, governments want enough infrastructure to maintain national power, China wants to close the gap, and the systems themselves are becoming more autonomous, more unpredictable and more difficult to monitor.The Hollywood version of this story ends with the machines taking over, but the real version may be messier: Humans are deciding how fast to build something they still do not fully understand while knowing that someone else is racing to build it first, and that makes the question of control as much about geopolitics, money and infrastructure as it is about the technology itself.Everyone agrees that the technology needs guardrails. The real test will come when following those guardrails means moving slower than a rival.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Balianta cops acted under pressure, arrested some innocent men in constable lynch case: Mishra
articles.summary: DGP Vinaytosh Mishra said Balianta police, under pressure, arrested innocents in GRP constable Soumya Swain lynching; crime branch chargesheeted 11.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: DGP (in-charge) Vinaytosh Mishra on Tuesday said Balianta police in Bhubaneswar had acted “under pressure” and arrested some “innocent” persons in connection with the mob lynching of railway constable Soumya Ranjan Swain in May. The case is currently being investigated by the crime branch.“Under pressure, the Balianta police arrested some accused on the basis of certain nicknames mentioned in the complaint. The crime branch subsequently found them to be innocent and did not include them in the chargesheet. The crime branch is not under any pressure and is conducting the investigation in a highly professional manner,” Mishra told reporters.Swain (32) was allegedly beaten to death by a mob at Balianta on May 7 after accusations surfaced that he had attempted to rape a 22-year-old woman by the roadside. Swain was assaulted in full public view and in the presence of police personnel, triggering widespread outrage. Following the incident, four police personnel were suspended and the then inspector in-charge of Balianta police station was transferred.A total of 20 men were arrested in connection with the case, with 11 arrested by Balianta police during the initial investigation and nine by the crime branch after it took over the probe on May 9.A senior officer of the commissionerate police, however, defended Balianta police action, saying, “We acted promptly and arrested the accused.”On Aug 5, the crime branch filed a chargesheet against 11 accused before the court of the sub-divisional judicial magistrate (SDJM). The remaining nine persons, who were earlier arrested by Balianta police, were not chargesheeted after investigators found insufficient evidence linking them to the crime.According to the crime branch, the chargesheet is based on oral evidence, documentary records, scientific findings and other corroborative materials collected during the investigation. articles.title: ED being used for political vendetta against Pinarayi Vijayan, says CPM’s A Vijayaraghavan
articles.summary: CPM leader A Vijayaraghavan alleges ED is used for political vendetta against Pinarayi Vijayan; party to review election setback and voting rights concerns.
articles.body: Kottayam: CPM politburo member A Vijayaraghavan on Tuesday said that enforcement directorate (ED) was being used to carry out political vendetta against leader of opposition Pinarayi Vijayan, and that the aim was to ‘eliminate’ CPM functionaries through accusations.Inaugurating the party’s extended district committee meeting in Pathanamthitta, Vijayaraghavan said an attempt was being made to implicate Vijayan in a bribery case. He alleged that sections of the media affected by ‘anti-communism’ were also behind the moves. He said ED had pursued Vijayan for 25 years and that nothing had come of the cases even after they reached Supreme Court. He accused Union govt of fostering a dangerous atmosphere of personal vendetta, and alleged that UDF govt in Kerala was colluding with it.Referring to the assembly election results, Vijayaraghavan said the Left had suffered a severe setback, with several CPM functionaries of popular standing losing. He also said that Congress had come to power in Keralam despite having little influence nationally. He said the party must examine its strengths and weaknesses and hold an intra-party discussion to address its limitations.He further alleged that the voting rights of minorities and scheduled castes were being denied across the country, and that Election Commission had removed crores of names from electoral rolls and created an atmosphere of fear. He said growing resistance was a source of hope and that CPM was able to stand at its forefront.Senior party member P J Ajayakumar presided over the meeting. State secretariat members P K Biju, P Rajeeve, V N Vasavan, M V Jayarajan, P Jayarajan and Saji Cherian; central committee member T M Thomas Isaac; former minister Veena George and district secretary Raju Abraham were among those present.A public meeting marking the conclusion of the meeting will be held at 5pm on Wednesday.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Suvendu arrives to vote on e-rick, speaks of ‘lifetime commitment’
articles.summary: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari votes in Nandigram bypoll, arriving by e-rickshaw; pledges to remain a local voter and predicts a record win margin.
articles.body: Nandigram: It’s not every day a chief minister rolls up to a polling booth in an e-rickshaw. Voters lined up outside Nandanayakbar Primary School were treated to quite the spectacle, getting their first up-close look at Suvendu Adhikari since he assumed office as the state’s CM.Greeting the voters, Adhikari said, “I will always remain a Nandigram voter.”“Under the rules, I cannot retain two assembly seats. I have kept Bhabanipur, but my commitment to Nandigram and Nandanayakbar remains lifelong. That is my pledge. I promise the people of Nandigram… until my last day, my name will remain on the voter list here. If I had given up Bhabanipur, it would have created an opportunity for someone else to contest there again — someone who had lost in 2021. There are able people here and I will handle the rest,” said the CM after casting his vote.Assuring people that he would be back soon, Adhikari said, “I come every year for Jagaddhatri Puja, and I will come this time as well. Since I hold the responsibility of governing the state, it may be difficult (to visit Nandigram regularly) — but I have not changed, and I never will.”Speaking of a big win margin, the CM said, “In 2016, I won by my highest margin – 82,000 votes. I believe that record will be broken this time. Bypolls usually see lower turnout, but I believe at least 85% will vote. It may even reach 90%.”Saying that the opposition was “missing in action” in Nandigram, Adhikari said, “No booth camps, no polling agents, nothing…the people of Nandigram may have seen them (opposition candidates) during campaigning, in the media, and with outsiders, but no one knows them.”On Tuesday, Adhikari left his East Midnapore residence around 10.45am. He arrived at Nandanayakbar Primary School polling station at 11.50am, travelling in an e-rickshaw for more than a kilometre as the cemented pathway is unsuitable for four-wheelers. His security followed in five rickshaws.In the five-odd minutes that Adhikari went inside and came out after casting his vote, hundreds had gathered on both sides of the cemented road. articles.title: HAL Koraput rolls out 2,000th engine, gets new Shakti line
articles.summary: HAL Koraput rolls out its 2,000th aero-engine as Rajnath Singh announces a Rs 218-crore second Shakti engine line and higher AL-31FP output.
articles.body: Koraput: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday described self-reliance in aero-engine technology as the foundation of India’s aerospace sovereignty as HAL’s Koraput division at Sunabeda rolled out its 2,000th aero-engine, marking six decades of propulsion manufacturing.Witnessing the milestone in the presence of Odisha chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi, Singh announced a Rs 218-crore second production line for Shakti helicopter engines at Sunabeda. The new line, scheduled to be fully established by 2028-29, will have the capacity to manufacture up to 100 engines annually for indigenous helicopters, including Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter (ALH) and Prachand Light Combat Helicopter (LCH).“Self-reliance in aero-engines is the foundation of India’s complete aerospace sovereignty,” Singh said, calling for strengthening indigenous capabilities in engine design, development, testing, manufacturing and maintenance.Congratulating the engineers, technicians and workforce of HAL Koraput, Singh said the delivery of the 2,000th engine represented 2,000 contributions to the operational capability of the armed forces. Established in 1964, the division has played a key role in India’s military aviation programme, with its engines powering frontline aircraft such as the MiG-21, MiG-27, MiG-29 and Su-30MKI.Besides manufacturing engines, HAL Koraput has overhauled more than 9,000 aero-engines. Singh said overhaul was equally important as production as it extends the operational life of critical defence assets and strengthens military preparedness.HAL will also raise its annual production capacity of AL-31FP engines from 30 to 50 with an investment of Rs 335 crore. The govt had placed an order for 240 AL-31FP engines for the Su-30MKI in 2024. Despite global supply-chain disruptions and raw-material challenges, HAL has delivered 63 engines against a target of 60 by the end of the second year.Describing the aero-engine as the “heart” of an aircraft, Singh said India needed to master advanced materials, metallurgy, precision manufacturing, cooling technologies, testing and quality assurance to achieve self-reliance in aerospace propulsion.He said the govt was pursuing an indigenous high-thrust engine programme, particularly for the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), with an investment of around Rs 5,000 crore. The programme includes indigenisation of raw materials in partnership with Mishra Dhatu Nigam Limited (MIDHANI) and establishment of India’s first indigenous high-thrust engine testing facility.Singh urged HAL to transform Koraput into a broader aerospace propulsion hub by developing suppliers, mentoring MSMEs, encouraging start-ups and collaborating with universities and research institutions.Highlighting Odisha’s growing strategic importance, Singh referred to the proposed Aerospace and Defence Equipment Manufacturing Complex at Gajamara in Dhenkanal. He said the Hindustan Shipyard Limited facility at Visakhapatnam and the new Shakti engine production line at Sunabeda would together strengthen eastern India’s industrial and strategic identity.Singh also called upon HAL Koraput to raise standards in quality, productivity, indigenisation and innovation, saying the 2,000th engine should serve as a foundation for building a stronger indigenous aerospace industry.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news. articles.title: Bill Clinton plays saxophone for musical birthday tribute to Václav Havel
articles.summary: More than three decades after picking up a saxophone for a famous musical moment in the Czech Republic, former President Clinton is dusting off the instrument once again as part of a tuneful tribute. “I’m really honored to join with people all across the Czech Republic and all around the world in observing the 90th birthday…
articles.body:
More than three decades after picking up a saxophone for a famous musical moment in the Czech Republic, former President Clinton is dusting off the instrument once again as part of a tuneful tribute.

“I’m really honored to join with people all across the Czech Republic and all around the world in observing the 90 th birthday of my friend, Václav Havel,” Clinton said in a video released Monday on social media.

“I will never forget that night more than 32 years ago now, when Havel took me to the jazz club in Prague,” Clinton said of Havel, the late Czech playwright and political dissident who in 1993 became the country’s first president.

In 1994, Clinton visited Prague, and Havel surprised the then-commander in chief with a trip to a jazz club before giving him a saxophone engraved with his signature and a heart. Clinton had famously shown off his sax skills two years earlier, while sporting a pair of “Blues Brothers”-esque shades in an appearance on “The Arsenio Hall Show” during his 1992 White House bid.

The pair of presidents then took part in an impromptu performance onstage in Prague. While Havel played the tambourine, Clinton jammed with the band on the sax on the jazz standards “My Funny Valentine” and “Summertime.”

“I think about him all the time — how kind he was, all the things we did together,” the 42 nd president said of Havel, who died in 2011.

Calling Havel “one of the most inspiring leaders that I ever worked with,” Clinton played a few notes of the song, “Happy Birthday.”

“I will always be grateful that I had a chance to support the Czech Republic in its blooming democracy and then in its leadership role in the expansion of NATO,” Clinton said.

“He was a special man for a special time and I’m glad to do what I can do observe his birthday.”

articles.title: Saudi-Israel normalization may come, but don’t expect a warm peace
articles.summary: While President Trump seeks to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia through civilian nuclear cooperation, significant social opposition and regional complexities suggest such an agreement may result in a cold peace rather than true reconciliation.
articles.body:
President Trump has made normalization with Israel a condition for moving forward with U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation, while Washington has deepened defense ties with Riyadh. The Saudis have not publicly accepted Trump’s quid pro quo and continue to demand meaningful progress toward Palestinian statehood.

Trump may accomplish during his remaining term what seemed impossible after Oct. 7, Saudi recognition of Israel. But Washington should not confuse a diplomatic breakthrough with a warm peace. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman may be ready for a strategic relationship with Israel, but Saudi society is not ready to embrace the Jewish state.

If diplomatic relations are eventually established, almost certainly with significant American influence, the critical question is what kind of relationship will follow.

Will it resemble Israel’s relatively warm relationship with the United Arab Emirates , which has survived the enormous strains since Oct. 7? Or will it look more like Israel’s cold peace with Egypt and Jordan, essential security cooperation accompanied by considerable public hostility?

Washington too often uses the word “peace” as though Middle Eastern normalization means something resembling relations between the United States and Canada. It does not. Regional governments must contend with conservative domestic politics, Islamist religious currents , ahistorical grievances, and populations whose attitudes toward Israel can be far more hostile than those of their rulers.

Saudi Arabia illustrates the problem. Bin Salman has dramatically modernized parts of the kingdom. But Saudi society is not Riyadh’s business elite, and its attitudes toward Israel present a formidable obstacle to an Emirati-style relationship.

Recent polling underscores the challenge. In 2025, 81 percent of Saudis surveyed viewed establishing normal, peaceful relations with Israel negatively, while only 13 percent viewed the Abraham Accords positively. After Oct. 7 , 96 percent favored Arab states cutting ties with Israel, illustrating the enormous gulf between Bin Salman’s strategic calculations and Saudi public opinion.

Israel and Saudi Arabia have quietly cooperated for years , sharing intelligence and coordinating against common adversaries, particularly Iran. For the foreseeable future, that may be closer to what Riyadh wants or believes it can politically sustain, than an Emirati-style embrace of Israel.

Disrupting Saudi-Israeli normalization served Hamas and Iran’s strategic interests on Oct. 7. Before the attack, there was considerable optimism that Saudi normalization could build upon the Abraham Accords , combining Israeli technology, intelligence and security capabilities with Saudi economic power.

Even if Trump persuades Bin Salman to resume normalization, the relationship will begin under vastly different circumstances. Washington should also think carefully before permitting Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium on its soil as a quid pro quo for diplomatic relations.

Saudi Arabia is stable today, but nuclear agreements must be designed for decades. Bin Salman will eventually succeed his father, King Salman, while members of the royal family remember being detained at the Ritz-Carlton during his consolidation of power. A future succession could produce significant instability. Creating an indigenous enrichment capability therefore carries proliferation risks extending well beyond today’s geopolitical calculations.

A future Israeli government may offer Riyadh sufficient movement on the Palestinian issue to facilitate normalization. But Israel can take immediate action on something far more manageable, extremist violence in the West Bank.

Israel confronts genuine Palestinian terrorism every day. That threat should not be minimized or equated with settler violence . But Israelis who attack innocent Palestinians, destroy property or violate Israeli law undermine their country’s strategic interests.

The Netanyahu government or the next one, should aggressively enforce Israeli law, including administrative detention when justified by security considerations, against the relatively small number of extremists responsible. Allowing their actions to continue creates an unnecessary diplomatic vulnerability when Israel needs to rebuild international and, most importantly, American support. European governments are increasing pressure over West Bank policies, while congressional Democrats have proposed sanctions connected to Israeli settlement activity.

For now, substantial public progress between Israel and Saudi Arabia is unlikely, particularly before Israel has a stable government following its elections. Yet Iran will continue pushing the two countries together. Shared threats from Tehran and the Houthis make Saudi-Israeli intelligence and security cooperation necessary, even if much remains in the shadows.

Riyadh must also calculate America’s long-term commitment to the region. Trump leaves office in January 2029, and neither Saudi Arabia nor Israel knows whether his successor, Democrat or Republican, will sustain the same level of engagement. American credibility and deterrence in the Middle East also reverberate in Beijing and Taipei.

Trump nevertheless should not be underestimated. The Abraham Accords overturned decades of conventional wisdom that Arab-Israeli normalization could not advance without first resolving the Palestinian conflict. He could surprise the region again.

But Saudi recognition of Israel, however historic, would not necessarily mean reconciliation. The more realistic relationship may resemble Egypt or Jordan : formal diplomatic relations and extensive security cooperation while societal normalization remains years, perhaps decades, away.

Jerusalem knows, and Washington should understand the difference between an agreement between governments and peace between peoples.

Eric R. Mandel is the director of the Middle East Political Information Network and senior security editor for the Jerusalem Post’s Jerusalem Report.

articles.title: Kemi Badenoch: I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK
articles.summary: The Conservative Party leader also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24 year olds.
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.

The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".

Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.

As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.

Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.

She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles .

Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.

She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win.

"The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority.

"My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."

A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election.

Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."

Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".

She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour . Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".

Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches .

Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received , including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.

Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down.

Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.

Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.

Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election , arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.

Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party" .

Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24.

The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice.

The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year.

On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job".

She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today."

The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.

They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21.

The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training.

Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first.

"So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it.

"If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else."

A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training".

articles.title: UN food agency official fired after highlighting Gaza hunger
articles.summary: Former United Nations food agency official Benjamin Davis said he was fired after his work, including briefs and seminars, highlighted the hunger crisis in Gaza, The Guardian reported Tuesday. The outlet wrote that the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) director’s seminar led the Israeli mission to file a complaint with the FAO. The mission also…
articles.body:
Former United Nations food agency official Benjamin Davis said he was fired after his work, including briefs and seminars, highlighted the hunger crisis in Gaza, The Guardian reported Tuesday.

The outlet wrote that the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) director’s seminar led the Israeli mission to file a complaint with the FAO. The mission also dispatched a diplomat to take photos of staff taking part in a moment of silence gathering in October 2025.

FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu requested Davis, a Spanish American citizen and a 26-year fixture within the FAO, step down from his role by Sept. 30. Davis appealed and rejected any notion that his actions were political.

“I feel it’s a terrible injustice,” he told Reuters last week. “I’ve been disciplined without due process for speaking about a subject at the core of FAO’s mandate about the right to food which is the most basic of human rights.”

The Hill has reached out to the FAO for comment.

Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal last Tuesday when he threatened to fire anyone considered to be engaging in political activism. He said at the 28th Session of the Committee on Forestry in Rome that the FAO is “not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” according to The Guardian.

“Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva,” he continued. “If you want to take care [of human rights], go there. That’s why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him. I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many.”

Davis told The Guardian that he and other FAO staff members were shocked by the remarks. He accused Qu of making comments about human rights that undermine “the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists.”

Davis wrote in his official response to his dismissal that silence “in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity.”

“Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate,” his letter reads, according to The Guardian. “Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.”

In September 2025, Davis said there was an altercation with a woman who identified herself as an Israeli diplomat. He told the British newspaper that she took photos of the meeting and that she later complained to FAO security that she was being harassed. Davis said these meetings, the moments of silence and the associated seminar were all approved by FAO management.

He said in an interview with The New Humanitarian that he wished some of the FAO’s senior management had attended the moments of silence and “step up.”

“But I tell people –– because a lot of people are bummed out, they don’t know what to do, they’re very disheartened –– I say, just do whatever little you can do,” he told the outlet. “Don’t despair.”

The Gaza Strip has faced worsening conditions in the nearly three years since Israel launched its military campaign across the territory in response to the Hamas-led attack on Israeli citizens on Oct. 7, 2023.

The territory’s roughly 2 million residents have endured a worsening hunger crisis amid the threat of Israeli strikes, drones, snipers and ground troops before and after the ceasefire deal reached last October. The war has led to the deaths of more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

articles.title: Some sugar-free Starbucks drinks have as much sugar as a Kit Kat bar, lawsuit says
articles.summary: A consumer lawsuit is accusing Starbucks of adding sugar, sometimes as much as that in a Kit Kat bar, to drinks marketed as sugar free.
articles.body: A consumer lawsuit is accusing Starbucks of adding sugar, sometimes as much as that in a Kit Kat bar, to drinks marketed as sugar free. The products in question include hot and iced protein lattes and protein matcha beverages in vanilla and caramel flavors. According to the federal lawsuit filed Friday, these drinks contain 13 to 21 grams of sugar per serving. “No reasonable person” would expect something labeled “sugar-free” to contain that much sugar, the lawsuit contends. “This case is about false and misleading product names. It is not about missing nutritional information,” according to the lawsuit. Starbucks denied misleading consumers with its menu in a statement to NBC News on Tuesday. The international coffee chain said it has “consistently and clearly provided information about its protein beverages, sugar-free options, customization choices, and nutritional content across product announcements, menus, marketing materials, Starbucks.com and the Starbucks app, and we intend to vigorously defend ourselves in this matter.” Hagens Berman filed the suit on behalf of three individual consumers who bought Starbucks’ sugar-free protein drinks in California, New York and Washington, The Associated Press reported. “Consumers avoid sugar for various reasons, whether that be general health, diabetes and blood glucose levels or other factors, and for many, a staunch mislabeling like this is significant,” Steve Berman, a co-founder and managing partner of the Seattle-headquartered firm, told the AP. Seattle-based Starbucks said the sugar in its protein drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk it uses. The company said it doesn’t add sugar to the drinks and it uses sugar-free syrup for flavoring. On Starbucks’ website Monday, the drinks were marketed as “sugar-free,” but the company also stated the amount of sugar in each beverage and that they were made without added sugar. The lawsuit seeks damages on behalf of U.S. consumers who bought the drinks. It also wants the court to order Starbucks to stop using the label “sugar-free” on products that contain sugar.

articles.title: Over 347M children under threat due to El Niño, UNICEF says
articles.summary: In previous years, millions were forced to leave their homes searching for food, water and work.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Millions of children around the world are facing the threat of one of the strongest El Niño events on record, according to UNICEF .

UNICEF reported that the unusual wet and dry conditions are expected to lead to extreme weather, including heavy flooding and severe droughts. As a result, the lives and health of over 347 million children in nearly 100 countries are under threat, the organization said.

“For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages and disease outbreaks.”

UNICEF reports children in Asia and the Pacific are likely to be the most affected, with around 190 children facing the threat. Around 41 million children are likely to be impacted in East and Southern Africa, and 41 million children in Latin America and the Caribbean.

In Europe and Central Asia, around 22 million children face the threat of El Niño. In the Middle East and Northern Africa, around 20 million children are expected to be impacted, as well as 20 million in West and Central Africa, according to UNICEF.

“Children are also at the risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship,” Russell said.

This is not the first time children have been at risk due to El Niño. According to the World Health Organization , the El Niño event of 2015-2016 impacted 60 million people across 23 countries.

Millions were forced to leave their homes searching for food, water and work after extreme weather heavily impacted their daily lives, Save the Children reported . At the time, around six million children were pushed into malnourishment.

This year’s El Niño can lead to drought and water scarcity, increasing the risk of displacement in places like Colombia, Fiji, Papua New Guinea and the Philippines, UNICEF said.

According to the organization, weather-related disasters have already displaced more than 20,000 children every day between 2016 and 2023.

PTI reported.In a statement, Pakistan Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the “weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.”According to the Pakistan army, the test validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability.Senior Pakistan army officers, together with scientists and engineers, were reportedly present to watch the launch.President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Asim Munir, who serves as Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces, and the services chiefs praised the successful test.Pakistan had previously carried out a successful test of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile in May.The base version of Fatah-4 reportedly has a range of up to 750 kilometres and can reportedly hit targets with a five-metre accuracy.The military confirmed the new variant has an extended range but did not clarify how far.Fatah-4 is a conventional cruise missile of Islamabad’s army rocket force command. articles.title: Someone may have hacked the North Korean UN mission’s voicemail
articles.summary: For the past 29 years, one of the few ways to get in touch with the North Korean government has been a phone number printed in the United Nations member directory.
articles.body: For the past 29 years, one of the few ways to get in touch with the North Korean government has been a phone number printed in the United Nations member directory. It’s the line to North Korea’s permanent mission to the UN — their only diplomatic outpost on American soil — an office on the 13th floor of a midtown Manhattan skyscraper. However, sometime within the past three years, an unknown person apparently hacked the mission’s voicemail, rerecording the greeting message as a satirical monologue about mass starvation and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. CNN discovered the voicemail in late September while attempting to contact the mission. Callers who dial its number and stay on for the voicemail greeting now hear a high-pitched voice speaking in a racist caricature of an East Asian accent. The speaker jokes about North Korea’s chronic food shortages and encourages anyone wishing to contact Kim Jong Un to leave a message, saying that if they do, perhaps “someone (will) get fed sometime soon.” Then an automated voice chimes in, informing the caller that the mailbox is full. Isolated North Korea has in the past faced huge food shortages driven by economic mismanagement and exacerbated by official clampdowns on border trade, as well as the diversion of scarce resources to military projects, according to experts. The North Korean mission did not answer an email inquiring about its voicemail greeting being changed. When a CNN producer went to their office in New York and knocked on the door to ask in person, a male staffer emerged. The staffer refused to answer questions but listened, with a surprised expression, as the producer called the mission’s number and played the voicemail greeting in its entirety. “This is not our number,” the staffer said and slammed the door shut. Days later, after North Korea’s vice foreign minister addressed the UN General Assembly, the mission published the phone number in question on the first page of the minister’s speech. As of writing, the greeting remains unchanged. A spokesperson for the UN Media and Liaison Unit (MALU) told CNN that the number connected to the voicemail was the only one they had, and that they were unaware of any change to the mission’s voicemail greeting. The UN’s Protocol and Liaison Service, which publishes the directory, referred CNN back to MALU. Cheap trick It’s unclear who pulled the prank, though there are a few public hints as to when it may have changed and how. David Maxwell, vice president at the Center for Asia Pacific Strategy, told CNN that he called the mission while attending a protest outside in November 2023. Maxwell recalled that the voicemail greeting at the time was just a recording informing the caller that the number did not take messages. Experts told CNN that finding out who changed the voicemail is impossible without access to the private call logs for the North Korean mission, but a stranger may have been able to re-record the mission’s greeting message without much effort. Barcelona-based cybersecurity researcher Martin Vigo told CNN that many users often fail to change their voicemail passwords from the default code issued by the carrier, which in some cases may be the last four digits of their phone number. Guessing passcodes is also rather easy, especially with automated calling services that can rapidly guess and input thousands of combinations for four-digit PINs. “For 40 bucks, I can 100% access your voicemail if you have a four-digit pin,” said Vigo. “It’s very cheap, and very fast.” ‘The New York channel’ The mission’s phone line once served as a key circuit for diplomacy. North Korea and the US have no formal ties, so the country’s UN mission long acted as “the New York channel”: one of the only points of contact between the US government and Pyongyang. Joel S. Wit, a former State Department official and author of a book on US attempts to disarm North Korea, said that the mission was an important part of negotiations over North Korea’s nuclear program in 1994. The mission has a permanent staff of 23 diplomats and aides, according to the UN’s directory. Wit remembers the mission’s office space as sparsely furnished with “the required picture of their leaders” hanging on the wall. All the mission staff live nearby, as the State Department requires North Korea’s diplomats to obtain permission before traveling more than 25 miles from New York City. “Back in the Clinton years, we were actually doing negotiations with the North Korean mission,” said Wit. “This was a very serious relationship.” But times have changed. Wit said that as succeeding attempts to defuse North Korea’s nuclear program have failed — including landmark talks in 2019 between Kim Jong Un and US President Donald Trump – Pyongyang and the US have lost what few diplomatic ties they had. Instead, North Korea has cultivated relations closer to home, especially with Russia, which has gladly accepted thousands of North Korean soldiers for the front lines of its war in Ukraine. “Ukraine is a prime example of the shift in relations,” Wit said. “The North Koreans think geopolitically. They’re not ideological robots. Their geopolitics drives their foreign policy.” “I’m sure that the New York channel today is pretty much non-functioning,” Wit continued. “Whoever hacked (the voicemail) probably didn’t know, but it’s a function of the relationship between the United States and North Korea. Today, the relationship doesn’t matter to the North Koreans.”

articles.title: Cabinet nod for B’luru police force to split into 5 units
articles.summary: Karnataka cabinet approves splitting Bengaluru police into five commissionerates—Central, East, West, North, South—under a chief commissioner; 1,022 new posts.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The Karnataka capital is all set to have a decentralised policing shield, with the state cabinet Tuesday granting its approval to break down the city‘s single police unit into five commissionerates — Central, East, West, North, and South — under a newly upgraded chief commissioner of police (CCP).Designed to streamline response time and traffic management, the plan aims to deploy 1,022 new personnel alongside a strategic redeployment of the existing force to offset staffing shortfalls.The restructuring will broadly be on the lines of the Greater Bengaluru Authority’s (GBA) five city corporations.Under the plan, each commissionerate will be headed by a police commissioner of IGP or DIG rank and report to a chief commissioner of police (CCP). The existing city police commissioner’s post will be upgraded to CCP.Home minister Priyank Kharge said the move was aimed at improving response, crime control, law and order and traffic management in a city with a population of over 1.5 crore.The existing commissionerate has 11 divisions, 116 police stations and 53 traffic police stations.The proposal, submitted by Bengaluru police commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh in Aug, came a year after GBA replaced BBMP, splitting the city’s civic administration into five corporations.The GBA model, however, has faced implementation hurdles. The five corporations have reported staff shortages, while concerns have also been flagged over funding, coordination, absence of elected councils, even as citizens continue to report problems with potholes, garbage, footpaths and drainage.In order to have five separate police commissionerates, there is a requirement of 6,550 additional personnel. The cabinet has shown the greenlight to 1,022 new personnel for now, with the remaining to be met through redeployment of existing personnel. In addition, 276 personnel have been sanctioned for 11 existing police stations, including those on the city’s outskirts.The original restructuring proposal had envisaged 6,633 additional posts and an expenditure of about Rs 765 crore.The new plan will see creation of six new ACP posts, with each ACP office having five executive posts.Personnel will also be redeployed from existing City Armed Reserve units (CAR), while a new CAR unit will be created for the East commissionerate.Points for info gfx:INSIDE THE REJIG* Central, East, West, North and South commissionerates to mirror GBA’s 5 city corporations* Each to be headed by an IGP/DIG-rank officer* Existing city police commissioner’s post to be upgraded to chief commissioner of police (CCP)* Five commissioners will report to CCP* Cabinet approves appointment of 1,022 new personnel* Another 276 personnel sanctioned for 11 existing police stations* Six new ACP posts to be createdYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news.
