articles.title: Steak 'n Shake makes major change to burger ingredient as chain continues MAHA push
articles.summary: Fast-food chain Steak 'n Shake now drenches all buns in pure "Grade AA Wisconsin butter" after ditching seed oils as part of the Make America Healthy Again push.
articles.body: Steak 'n Shake is now ridding its buns of seed oils. "Starting today, all Steak 'n Shake buns are officially seed-oil free," the fast-food chain announced Monday in a post on X. "The buns are now unapologetically drenched in pure Grade AA Wisconsin butter." The bun change is the latest in a series of moves by Steak 'n Shake, which has about 400 locations nationwide, to overhaul its ingredients and align itself with the MAHA movement. STEAK 'N SHAKE TAPS MAHA OFFICER AS FAST-FOOD CHAIN JOINS RFK JR'S PUSH TO OVERHAUL AMERICAN DIET In June, Steak 'n Shake made the switch to grass-fed beef and began frying chicken tenders, onion rings and tots in 100% beef tallow. "In my opinion, real ingredients taste better than the synthetic additives," Michael Boes, the chain's chief MAHA officer, told Fox News. The chain also has a page on its website dedicated to its transition away from seed oils and its efforts to provide more natural ingredients. Aside from a "commitment to remove seed oils," the page touts offering cane sugar Coca-Cola and its switch to a2 milk last December. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Reaction to the news was largely positive. "MAKE AMERICA HEALTHY AGAIN," U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., commented on X. Another X user wrote, "Thank you for listening to the people! Amazing." "I haven't enjoyed one of your burgers in quite some time," one commenter said. "I look forward to trying this change!" Seed oils — plant-based cooking oils that are regularly used in processed and packaged foods — are a hot topic in the food and nutrition landscape. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS U.S. Health and Human Services (HSS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken critic of seed oils. Other health agencies have said that seed oils are not so bad. The American Heart Association (AHA) stated in 2024 that "there's no reason to avoid seed oils and plenty of reasons to eat them." Board-certified family physician Cate Shanahan told Fox News Digital in 2025 that while some seed oils, such as flax oil and sesame seed oil, have nutritional value, there are certain varieties of which people should steer clear. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Shanahan advised that Americans try to stay away from what she calls "the hateful eight seed oils," which include corn, canola, cottonseed, soy, sunflower, safflower, rice bran and grapeseed. articles.title: Trump blames French student protests on Islam, ‘out of control mass migration’
articles.summary: President Trump blamed the widespread student-led protests in France on Islam and “out of control mass migration” on Tuesday. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.…
articles.body:
President Trump blamed the widespread student-led protests in France on Islam and “out of control mass migration” on Tuesday.

“What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country,” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Student protests have called for more teachers and better schooling facilities, as neither immigration nor religion have been included in their demands, according to The New York Times .

Since late last month, protests have popped up across France, which has caused clashes with police and school officials. The protests began Sept. 21 at a high school in a suburb of Paris over teacher shortages and deteriorating building conditions.

One student, Issam Makhloufi, described conditions in the classroom as “not ventilated,” and that students “can barely open the windows,” per The Times.

Since the start of the protests, more than 100 students, police officers and demonstrators have been injured, while Education Minister Édouard Geffray told France 2 at least 24 schools have been ransacked or set on fire.

A 15-year-old reportedly lost his lower arm and hand after he picked up and detonated a police stun grenade, newspaper La Voix du Nord reported. At least one student lost teeth and others suffered eye injuries during the protests, according to the BBC .

It is unclear when the protests may end, as France’s justice minister Gérald Darmanin said, “one of the difficulties of this movement is that there are no national demands. It all started with local demands.”

Conservatives have echoed Trump’s point, blaming the European Union’s (EU) immigration policies for the protests.

“I would also say as we’re sitting here in beautiful New York City, this is a cautionary tale,” Fox News co-host Tomi Lahren said on “The Big Weekend Show.”

In June, the EU enacted an overhaul of its immigration system , increasing deportations and beginning construction on detention centers abroad. Critics of the overhaul compared it to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the U.S. which has detained a record number of people in Trump’s second term.

French President Emmanuel Macron also alleged in January that Trump wanted to “weaken and subordinate” Europe, adding in February that the Trump administration was “openly anti-European.”

Macron’s comments spill over into issues including Trump’s push to acquire Greenland and his tariff policies.

articles.title: US arrest announced in connection with Canada’s Tumbler Ridge school shooting
articles.summary: US authorities have announced the arrest of a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
articles.body: US authorities have announced the arrest of a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. The person, identified by authorities as James Cody Bryant, was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to an announcement by the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town of Tumbler Ridge was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead and dozens wounded. Bryant was scheduled to appear in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle, according to a press release ahead of the announcement. CNN has not yet confirmed whether Bryant has legal representation. Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money, and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle. The money amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but ultimately Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so, authorities alleged. Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school. Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference. Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.” “As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.” It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned. CNN’s Josh Campbell and Paula Newton contributed reporting. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: How drunk is too drunk? Cornell rape allegations expose 'loopholes' in consent laws
articles.summary: The BBC speaks to experts about current US state sexual assault laws and why some believe changing them will help alleged victims.
articles.body:
A backlash over the handling of a US woman's sexual assault complaint against Cornell University fraternity members has highlighted what experts believe are issues with the current laws in many states regarding sexual assault and drinking.

The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, last month filed a lawsuit alleging she was drugged and raped by several men in 2024 at the university in the state of New York.

Doe said she had been drinking earlier in the evening of the alleged incident and then went to a fraternity house, where several men pressured her to snort the drug ketamine and plied her with alcohol before advertising a "free" sexual encounter with her in a group message.

She said she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

Under current New York law, a person who voluntarily consumes drugs or alcohol - rather than becoming intoxicated without their consent - is not automatically considered unable to consent to sex.

US media has been widely reporting it as the "voluntary intoxication loophole".

New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week said: "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape" and that she would work with the state legislature to close the "loophole".

But some experts say the law has been misinterpreted and that it does not stop people who choose to consume alcohol or drugs from reporting sexual assault. It does, however, require them to prove they were so incapacitated they could not physically consent - a higher bar than being intoxicated.

The distinction reflects an ongoing debate in the US about what counts as consent when someone has been drinking.

Dan Schorr, a former sex crimes prosecutor, told the BBC that New York law still protects victims of assaults who have chosen to drink or take drugs.

"If a person cannot express consent or lack of consent due to the consumption of alcohol or drugs, any sexual activity with them is always non-consensual, whether the ingestion of alcohol or drugs was voluntary or involuntary," said Schorr, who also helps universities review sexual assault cases.

"I prosecuted many people who sexually assaulted someone who was voluntarily intoxicated," he said, adding: "I got convictions. They went to prison."

What we know about Cornell University frat house rape investigation

Some believe issue with the current law is that the bar is set too high with regards to what counts as being too intoxicated to give consent.

At least 19 states, including New York, have a higher bar for the level of intoxication required to deem someone incapacitated and unable to consent.

The New York law includes a provision that someone cannot consent to sex if they are "unconscious or for any other reason physically unable to communicate an unwillingness to an act".

This applies to people who are too incapacitated from drinking to consent, Schorr said.

But another legal expert the BBC spoke to says that can be difficult to prove.

Some prosecutors "may not bring charges or defendants may be acquitted because someone 'gave consent' while intoxicated, but not completely incapacitated", according to Mitchell Epner, a former prosecutor who has handled sex trafficking cases.

He said that in other states that have lower legal bars for incapacitation, someone who is "impaired" or "significantly impaired" cannot consent, and that being too drunk to drive a car could be considered as being at this level.

College campuses have different standards for consent than criminal law, including Cornell, which uses a standard of affirmative consent, defined as "a knowing, voluntary, and mutual decision among all participants to engage in sexual activity". Cornell says silence or lack of resistance does not constitute consent.

'Ashamed': Cornell students gather to voice anger over alleged gang rape

Epner supports a proposed change to New York's law to widen the scope of when someone is too intoxicated to consent. The New York Senate has passed a bill multiple times, but the state Assembly failed to bring it up for a vote.

That bill states that people cannot give consent if they are under the influence of substances that have rendered them "temporarily incapable of appraising or controlling" their conduct, and "such conduct was known or reasonably should have been known" to the other person.

Pennsylvania has also made efforts to try and change the law to make it easier for victims who were intoxicated to prove they were assaulted.

"If somebody's too drunk to drive, they're too drunk to - fill in your verb of choice," Epner said.

Representative Lea Webb, whose district includes Cornell University, told the BBC News Channel she and her fellow lawmakers were working to push through legislation on the issue, which has gone through several amendments.

New York's current laws, she said, "puts the onus of proof on the victim".

Schorr and criminal defence attorneys, meanwhile, criticised the proposed changes to New York's sexual assault laws.

New York's State Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers said in a statement to the BBC New York's current laws were sufficient, and that "people have been convicted of rape in cases involving voluntarily intoxicated victims".

The group said using language that a victim was "incapable of appraising or controlling their conduct" was "simply too vague to be fairly enforced", adding that the legislation does not give clear details on what constitutes someone being too intoxicated to engage in sexual conduct.

Schorr said it was not easy to answer this question of what exact point someone is too intoxicated to consent.

He added: "How should the law address that? It is very challenging to find a clear standard that will be evenly applied."

"It's a conversation we should have as a society, as a state".
